# Constant belt squeak

A persistent serpentine belt squeal on a 2002 GMC Sierra 2500HD, particularly one that appears only after water pump and hose replacement, points to a specific class of mechanical faults rather than simple component fatigue. The fact that the shop has already cycled through eight belts without resolving the issue suggests the root cause is not the belt itself, but the interaction between the belt and the tensioning system or pulley alignment. When a shop replaces the water pump and heater hoses, they often neglect to inspect the bearing surfaces of adjacent accessories or the condition of the idler/tensioner pulleys with the same rigor.

The most common culprit in this scenario is the tensioner assembly itself. On many GM trucks of this era, the hydraulic tensioner relies on an internal seal to maintain pressure against the belt. If that seal was compromised during the water pump replacementâperhaps due to debris left in the serpentine system or a dropped wrench impacting the pulleyâthe tensioner may have lost its ability to apply consistent clamping force. A weak tensioner allows the belt to whip slightly under load, creating friction noise that sounds like a high-pitched squeal. This often manifests intermittently because the engine RPM fluctuates; at idle, the belt might sit loosely enough to chirp, but under acceleration, the increased torque temporarily pushes the belt tighter against the pulleys, masking the noise until the system cools or the hydraulic pressure drops further.

Another frequent issue arises from the idler pulley bearings. Even if the shop claimed the pulleys were fine, a bearing can be in a transitional state of failure. A healthy bearing spins with zero resistance and no play. A failing bearing often exhibits "stiffness" at certain rotational speeds, causing the belt to slip momentarily before gripping again. To diagnose this without disassembly, you can perform a visual inspection while the engine is running (ensure safety precautions are taken). Use a piece of chalk or a marker to draw a line on the back of the belt and watch which pulleys cause the chalk mark to smear unevenly or if the belt skips a tooth on a grooved pulley. If the belt tracks erratically, the alignment of the idler brackets is suspect. Misaligned brackets force the belt to rub against the inner sides of adjacent pulleys, generating heat and noise that mimics belt slippage.

The water pump replacement itself introduces a variable: contamination. During the removal of the old pump, coolant debris or metal shavings from the gasket surface can fall into the serpentine belt path. Even microscopic particles can act as abrasives between the rubber compound and the pulley grooves. Over time, this grinds down the ribbing on the belt, reducing its traction and causing it to slip whenever torque demand increases. The solution here isn't another belt; it is a thorough cleaning of the entire accessory drive system using a dedicated brake cleaner or an electrical contact cleaner that evaporates quickly, leaving no residue.

There is also the possibility of a misaligned alternator bracket. On heavy-duty trucks like the Sierra 2500HD, the alternator is mounted on a long bracket that can warp under heat cycles. If the bracket has shifted even a few degrees out of alignment, the belt runs at an angle rather than squarely across the pulleys. This angled run-up creates uneven wear and significant squealing. To check this, lock the wheels, start the engine, and observe the belt path from above while idling. If you see the belt bowing significantly off-center on any pulley, the mounting points for that accessory need adjustment or replacement.

Finally, consider the possibility of a seized accessory bearing. While less likely to be missed by a professional shop, if one of the power steering pump, alternator, or A/C compressor bearings has developed internal drag, it resists rotation. The belt must slip over this high-resistance point to keep turning, resulting in noise. Replacing the entire assembly is often necessary because these bearings are frequently press-fit and difficult to separate without destroying the unit. If the squeak persists after cleaning and verifying alignment, replacing the tensioner and idler pulleys as a complete kit is the most cost-effective way to rule out bearing failure across the board.
